questions.topic: Nature and branches of Art and careers in art
questions.stem: Painting and sculpture are usually grouped under
questions.explanation: Fine art is made mainly for aesthetic and expressive value; painting and sculpture are its classic branches. Applied art serves a practical function.

questions.topic: Nature and branches of Art and careers in art
questions.stem: Which of the following is a branch of applied art?
questions.explanation: Graphic design serves a practical purpose (communication, packaging, advertising), so it is applied art; the others are fine art.

questions.topic: Nature and branches of Art and careers in art
questions.stem: A person employed by a museum to acquire, care for and arrange works of art for exhibition is called
questions.explanation: A curator manages a collection and plans exhibitions; a critic evaluates and writes about art.

questions.stem: The element of art that describes how the surface of an object feels or appears to feel is
questions.explanation: Texture is actual or implied surface quality (rough, smooth, coarse).

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs are complementary colours?
questions.explanation: Complementary colours lie opposite each other on the wheel: blue is opposite orange (red + yellow).

questions.stem: Mixing a colour with grey, rather than with pure white or pure black, produces a
questions.explanation: White gives a tint, black gives a shade, and grey gives a tone (a duller version of the hue).

questions.stem: The difference between shape and form in art is that
options: shape is always geometric while form is always organic
shape has volume while form is flat
shape is made only with colour while form is made only with line
shape is two-dimensional while form is three-dimensional
questions.explanation: Shape has length and width only; form adds depth or volume (actual or implied).

questions.stem: A painter wants a bright red to look duller without changing its hue or making it lighter. The most suitable method is to add a little of its
questions.explanation: Adding a small amount of the complement reduces intensity (chroma) while keeping the hue; adding white would make it lighter.

questions.stem: In the colour wheel, the intensity (chroma) of a colour refers to its
questions.explanation: Intensity is the purity or saturation of a hue; lightness/darkness is value.

questions.stem: When the two halves of a composition are identical in arrangement on either side of a central line, the balance is
questions.explanation: Formal or symmetrical balance mirrors the elements on both sides of an axis.

questions.stem: The principle of art that creates a feeling of visual movement through the regular repetition of elements is
questions.explanation: Repetition of lines, shapes or colours at intervals produces rhythm.

questions.stem: In a poster, the name of a product is printed much larger and in a brighter colour than everything else. The principle applied is
questions.explanation: Making one element stand out through size or colour creates a focal point: emphasis.

questions.stem: A design in which petals, spokes or lines spread outward from a central point shows
questions.explanation: Radial balance arranges elements around a centre, as in a wheel or flower.

questions.stem: In linear perspective, parallel lines going away from the viewer appear to meet at the
questions.explanation: Receding parallel lines converge at a vanishing point on the eye level.

questions.stem: Distant hills in a landscape painting are made paler, bluer and less detailed than nearby objects. This technique is called
questions.explanation: Aerial perspective imitates the effect of the atmosphere, which softens and cools distant colours.

questions.stem: A drawing of a box viewed from one corner, showing two sets of receding edges converging at two points, uses
questions.explanation: Viewing a box corner-on gives two vanishing points: angular or two-point perspective.

questions.stem: An arm pointing directly at the viewer appears shorter than its real length in a drawing. This effect is known as
questions.explanation: Foreshortening shortens a form that is angled towards or away from the viewer to show depth.

questions.topic: Art and craft tools and materials
questions.stem: Which tool is used to hold a canvas or drawing board upright while the artist works?
questions.explanation: An easel supports the canvas or board; a palette holds paints.

questions.topic: Art and craft tools and materials
questions.stem: Brushes used with oil paint are best cleaned with
questions.explanation: Oil paint does not dissolve in water; turpentine or white spirit removes it, followed by soap and water.

questions.topic: Art and craft tools and materials
questions.stem: A fixative is sprayed on charcoal and pastel drawings in order to
questions.explanation: Charcoal and pastel are powdery; fixative binds the particles to the paper.

questions.topic: Art and craft tools and materials
questions.stem: Which of the following pencils would give the darkest and softest line?
questions.explanation: B grades are soft and dark (higher number = softer); H grades are hard and light.

questions.topic: Art and craft tools and materials
questions.stem: A rubber roller used to spread printing ink evenly on a lino block is called a
questions.explanation: The brayer rolls ink onto relief blocks; a squeegee pushes ink through a screen.

questions.stem: A dark outline shape of a person or object seen against a lighter background is called a
questions.explanation: A silhouette shows only the outline filled with one dark tone.

questions.stem: Pottery that has been fired once, without glaze, is known as
questions.explanation: Biscuit or bisque ware is clay after the first firing; greenware is unfired.

questions.stem: The soft, hazy blending of tones without sharp outlines, associated with Leonardo da Vinci, is
questions.explanation: Sfumato ("smoky") blends tones imperceptibly; chiaroscuro is strong light-dark contrast.

questions.stem: In photography, the adjustable opening in the lens that controls the amount of light entering the camera is the
questions.explanation: The aperture is the opening; the shutter controls how long light is let in.

questions.stem: During a dance-drama, masks, costumes and stage backdrops are mainly contributions of
questions.explanation: Visual artists design and make the costumes, masks, props and scenery used in drama and dance.

questions.stem: Which of the following best shows the link between visual art and the literary arts?
options: Composing the music for a play
Illustrating the pages of a storybook
Recording a song in a studio
questions.explanation: Book illustration translates written text into images, linking visual and literary arts.

questions.topic: Art of West Africa: general concepts
questions.stem: The belief that natural objects such as trees, rivers and rocks possess spirits is known as
questions.explanation: Animism attributes souls or spirits to natural objects and phenomena.

questions.topic: Art of West Africa: general concepts
questions.stem: An object believed to hold magical or spiritual power, which may be carved for protection, is called a
questions.explanation: Fetishism is the belief that certain made objects possess supernatural power.

questions.topic: Art of West Africa: general concepts
questions.stem: Which of the following is a secular function of traditional West African art?
options: Housing the spirit of an ancestor
Decorating household utensils such as stools and bowls
Representing a deity in a shrine
questions.explanation: Secular functions are non-religious, such as decoration of everyday objects; the others are sacred.

questions.topic: Art of West Africa: general concepts
questions.stem: A typical characteristic of traditional West African sculpture is
options: stylisation, with an enlarged head in relation to the body
strict photographic realism of the whole figure
preference for oil paint on canvas
questions.explanation: Traditional sculptures are often stylised, with the head enlarged because it is regarded as the seat of wisdom and life force.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: Nok terracotta sculptures were first discovered during
options: the building of a palace in Benin
the digging of a well in Igbo-Ukwu
tin mining on the Jos Plateau area
questions.explanation: Nok figures came to light in 1943 when tin miners found terracotta pieces near the village of Nok.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: Perforated pupils, elaborate hairstyles and triangular or D-shaped eyes are features of
questions.explanation: Nok heads have pierced pupils, stylised eyes and elaborate coiffures.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: The naturalistic heads of Ife are well known for
options: fine vertical striations (lines) on the face
questions.explanation: Many Ife heads are naturalistic portraits with fine parallel striations across the face.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: The Esie sculptures of Kwara State are made of
questions.explanation: Esie is noted for a large collection of soapstone figures, kept in the Esie Museum.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: The guild of bronze casters responsible for royal art in Benin is known as
questions.explanation: The Igun Eronmwon guild of brass casters worked for the Oba of Benin.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: The Chi Wara (Tyi Wara) antelope headdress, danced to honour farming, is associated with the
questions.explanation: The Bambara (Bamana) of Mali dance Chi Wara headdresses at farming ceremonies.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: The black, glossy helmet mask with rings around the neck, worn by women of the Sande society, belongs to the
questions.explanation: The Sowei helmet mask of the Mende Sande society is black and shiny, with neck rings suggesting beauty and health.

questions.topic: Modern Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: Bida in Niger State is well known for
questions.explanation: Nupe craftsmen in Bida are noted for decorated brass and copper work.

questions.topic: Modern Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: Mbari houses with painted mud sculptures were built by the Owerri Igbo in honour of
questions.explanation: Mbari houses were built as sacrifices to Ala, the earth deity, and filled with mud figures.

questions.topic: Modern Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: The pottery training centre at Abuja (now Suleja) was founded by
questions.explanation: Michael Cardew founded the Abuja Pottery Training Centre in the early 1950s; Ladi Kwali trained there.

questions.topic: Modern Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem: Adinkra cloth is decorated by
options: weaving narrow strips on a loom
tying and dyeing with indigo only
stamping symbols with carved calabash stamps
questions.explanation: Adinkra symbols are carved on calabash stamps and printed on cloth with a dark dye; kente is woven.

questions.topic: Art institutions, organisations and cultural festivals
questions.stem: FESTAC '77, held in Lagos, used as its emblem a replica of
options: the Benin ivory mask of Queen Idia
the Ife bronze head of Olokun
questions.explanation: The FESTAC '77 emblem was based on the 16th-century ivory pendant mask of Queen Idia of Benin.

questions.topic: Art institutions, organisations and cultural festivals
questions.stem: SNA, an important art organisation in Nigeria, stands for
questions.explanation: The Society of Nigerian Artists is the professional body of practising artists in Nigeria.

questions.topic: Art institutions, organisations and cultural festivals
questions.stem: The Ulli (Uli) art movement, which uses traditional Igbo body and wall-painting motifs, is associated mainly with
questions.explanation: Uche Okeke and others at Nsukka developed modern art from Uli motifs.

questions.stem: The famous sculpture "Anyanwu" was produced by
questions.explanation: Ben Enwonwu created Anyanwu, a bronze figure representing the rising sun.

questions.stem: Bruce Onobrakpeya is best known for his contributions to
options: printmaking, including plastography and deep etching
questions.explanation: Onobrakpeya developed printmaking techniques such as plastography and deep etching.

questions.stem: The Ghanaian-born sculptor who taught at Nsukka and became famous for large hangings made from metal bottle caps is
questions.explanation: El Anatsui creates shimmering wall hangings from aluminium bottle tops linked with copper wire.

questions.stem: Paintings on the walls of caves such as Lascaux and Altamira were made by
questions.explanation: These are Palaeolithic cave paintings by prehistoric hunters.

questions.stem: The main subjects of Palaeolithic cave painting were
options: animals such as bison, horses and deer
questions.explanation: Cave art mainly shows animals that were hunted, probably linked to hunting magic.

questions.stem: Pre-historic painters obtained their colours mainly from
options: earth pigments (ochres) and charcoal mixed with fat or water
questions.explanation: Ochres (red, yellow, brown) and charcoal (black) were ground and bound with animal fat, saliva or water.

questions.stem: The pyramids of Giza were built during the
questions.explanation: The Great Pyramids at Giza date to the Old Kingdom (4th Dynasty).

questions.stem: The main reason ancient Egyptians placed statues and paintings in tombs was
options: their belief in life after death
questions.explanation: Egyptians believed the ka (life force) needed images and goods to live on after death.

questions.stem: The intact tomb of Tutankhamun, discovered in 1922, belongs to which period of Egyptian history?
questions.explanation: Tutankhamun ruled during the 18th Dynasty of the New Kingdom; Howard Carter found his tomb in 1922.

questions.stem: The three orders of Greek architecture are
questions.explanation: The Greek orders are Doric, Ionic and Corinthian; Archaic, Classical and Hellenistic are periods.

questions.stem: Stiff standing male statues with one foot forward and a fixed "smile" are typical of the
questions.explanation: The kouros figures with the "archaic smile" belong to the Archaic period.

questions.stem: Dramatic emotion, twisting movement and realistic suffering, as seen in the Laocoon group, are features of
questions.explanation: Hellenistic sculpture favoured movement, drama and intense emotion.

questions.stem: Pointed arches, flying buttresses and large stained-glass windows are features of
questions.explanation: Gothic builders used pointed arches and buttresses to make tall walls with large windows.

questions.stem: Hand-written books decorated with gold, silver and bright colours in the Middle Ages are called
questions.explanation: Monks produced illuminated manuscripts, such as the Book of Kells.

questions.stem: The painting "Mona Lisa" was produced by
questions.explanation: Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa in the early 16th century.

questions.stem: The architect credited with working out the rules of linear perspective in the early fifteenth century is
questions.explanation: Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective in Florence; Masaccio applied it in painting.

questions.stem: Donatello's bronze "David" is important because it was
options: one of the first free-standing nude statues since ancient times
the first oil painting on canvas
a ceiling fresco in a chapel
questions.explanation: Donatello's David revived the free-standing nude figure of classical antiquity.

questions.stem: The name "Impressionism" was taken from a painting by
questions.explanation: A critic mocked Monet's "Impression, Sunrise" and the name stuck to the group.

questions.stem: Impressionist painters were mainly concerned with
options: capturing the changing effects of light and atmosphere
questions.explanation: Impressionists painted outdoors with quick broken brushstrokes to record light at a moment.

questions.stem: The painter famous for swirling, thick brushstrokes in works such as "The Starry Night" is
questions.explanation: Van Gogh used vigorous impasto strokes and expressive colour.

questions.stem: Paul Gauguin is particularly associated with paintings of
options: the people and landscapes of Tahiti in flat, bold colours
questions.explanation: Gauguin worked in Tahiti, using flat areas of strong, non-naturalistic colour.

questions.stem: "Les Demoiselles d'Avignon", regarded as a starting point of Cubism, was painted by
questions.explanation: Picasso painted it in 1907, partly influenced by African masks.

questions.stem: Cubist artists such as Picasso and Braque were influenced by African sculpture mainly in its
questions.explanation: African masks showed how forms could be simplified and reorganised geometrically.

questions.stem: In drawing a group of bottles, the lightest area where light strikes the shiny surface most directly is the
questions.explanation: The highlight is the brightest spot; the cast shadow falls on the surface beside the object.

questions.stem: When drawing a standing adult figure, artists commonly use the head as a unit, with the whole figure measuring about
options: seven and a half to eight heads
questions.explanation: A standard adult proportion is about 7.5 to 8 head-lengths tall.

questions.stem: Building up tone with closely spaced parallel lines crossed by another set of lines is called
questions.explanation: Cross-hatching layers crossed lines; stippling uses dots.

questions.stem: Lino cut and woodcut are examples of
questions.explanation: In relief printing the raised (uncut) surface receives the ink.

questions.stem: Letters cut on a lino block must be cut in reverse because
options: ink only sticks to reversed letters
the gouge can cut only backwards
the printed image is a mirror image of the block
questions.explanation: Printing flips the image, so text must be reversed on the block to read correctly.

questions.stem: Letters that have small finishing strokes at the ends of their main strokes are called
questions.explanation: Serifs are small projecting strokes, as in Roman letters; sans serif letters lack them.

questions.stem: The small pieces of tile, glass or stone used in making a mosaic are called
questions.explanation: Tesserae are the individual pieces set together to form a mosaic.

questions.stem: A photogram is produced by
options: photographing a person in a studio
printing a photograph by screen printing
placing objects on light-sensitive paper and exposing it to light without a camera
drawing on a photograph with pencil
questions.explanation: A photogram is a cameraless image made by objects blocking light on photographic paper.

questions.stem: The supporting framework of wire or wood built inside a clay or papier-mache figure is called
questions.explanation: An armature supports soft modelling materials so the figure keeps its shape.

questions.stem: Decorating a calabash by burning designs into its surface with a heated metal point is known as
questions.explanation: Pyrography uses a hot tool to burn lines and tones into a calabash or wood.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a three-dimensional craft product?
questions.explanation: A basket has length, width and depth; the others are two-dimensional works.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the following terms as used in colour: (i) primary colours; (ii) secondary colours; (iii) tertiary colours. [6 marks]
(b) Name two pairs of complementary colours. [2 marks]
(c) Explain, with one example each, the difference between warm and cool colours and the effect each has in a painting. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Primary: colours that cannot be obtained by mixing other colours: red, yellow, blue
2 marks: Secondary: obtained by mixing two primaries in equal amounts: orange, green, violet
2 marks: Tertiary: a primary mixed with a neighbouring secondary, e.g. yellow-green, red-orange
2 marks: Any two pairs: red-green, blue-orange, yellow-violet (1 mark each)
2 marks: Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) explained with example
2 marks: Cool colours (blue, green, violet) explained with example
3 marks: Effect: warm colours appear to advance and suggest heat, excitement or energy; cool colours recede and suggest calm, distance or coolness
questions.explanation: Primaries cannot be mixed; secondaries mix two primaries; tertiaries mix a primary and an adjacent secondary. Complementary pairs: red/green, blue/orange, yellow/violet. Warm colours advance and excite; cool colours recede and calm.

questions.stem:
(a) What is perspective in drawing? [2 marks]
(b) Explain the following: (i) parallel (one-point) perspective; (ii) angular (two-point) perspective; (iii) aerial perspective. [9 marks]
(c) State four rules that an artist should observe when drawing a street scene in linear perspective. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Perspective: method of representing three-dimensional objects and depth on a flat surface so they appear as seen by the eye
3 marks: Parallel perspective: object faces viewer squarely; receding lines meet at one vanishing point on the eye level
3 marks: Angular perspective: object seen from a corner; two sets of receding lines meet at two vanishing points on the eye level
3 marks: Aerial perspective: distant objects shown paler, bluer/greyer, with less detail and contrast
4 marks: Any four rules (1 each): objects get smaller as they recede; receding parallel lines converge at vanishing point(s); vanishing points lie on eye level/horizon; vertical lines remain vertical; nearer objects overlap farther ones; spacing between equal objects decreases with distance
questions.explanation: Perspective creates the illusion of depth. One-point: one VP; two-point: object at an angle with two VPs; aerial: atmosphere makes distance paler and bluer. Rules: diminishing size, convergence to VPs on the eye level, verticals stay vertical, overlapping.

questions.stem:
(a) List four tools and materials needed for making a lino print. [4 marks]
(b) Describe the stages involved in producing a single-colour lino print, from design to finished print. [8 marks]
(c) State three safety precautions to observe while cutting lino. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Any four (1 each): lino block, lino cutters/gouges (V and U), printing ink, brayer/roller, inking slab/glass, printing paper, baren/spoon or press, pencil/tracing paper, bench hook
2 marks: Prepare design and transfer it in reverse onto the lino (warming lino if hard)
2 marks: Cut away the parts that are to remain white (non-printing areas) with gouges
2 marks: Roll out ink evenly on slab and ink the block with a brayer
2 marks: Place paper on block, rub with baren/spoon or press, peel off print and dry; sign and number
3 marks: Any three (1 each): cut away from the body; keep the free hand behind the cutting edge; use a bench hook; keep tools sharp; store tools properly after use
questions.explanation: Lino print: design reversed onto block, non-printing areas cut away, ink rolled on with a brayer, paper pressed and peeled. Cut away from the body and use a bench hook.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem:
Write notes on Nok culture under the following headings:
(a) location and discovery; [4 marks]
(b) material and approximate date; [3 marks]
(c) characteristics of the sculptures. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Location: Nok village and surrounding area in southern Kaduna/Jos Plateau region, central Nigeria
2 marks: Discovery: by tin miners in the 1940s (1943), later studied by Bernard Fagg
2 marks: Material: terracotta (fired clay)
1 mark: Date: roughly 500 BC to AD 200 (accept about 900 BC to AD 300)
8 marks: Any four characteristics, 2 marks each: cylindrical/spherical or conical heads; triangular or D-shaped eyes with perforated pupils; elaborate hairstyles; heads large in proportion to body; perforated nostrils and ears; stylised rather than naturalistic; figures wearing beads/ornaments; human and animal subjects
questions.explanation: Nok terracottas were found by tin miners near Nok (Jos Plateau area) in 1943. They are fired clay, roughly 500 BC to AD 200, with stylised heads, pierced pupils, triangular eyes, elaborate coiffures and large heads.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem:
(a) Name two materials used by Benin artists apart from bronze/brass. [2 marks]
(b) Describe the lost-wax (cire perdue) process of casting a brass head. [8 marks]
(c) State five functions of Benin court art. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Any two: ivory, wood, terracotta, iron, coral beads (1 each)
2 marks: A clay core is shaped and covered with a layer of wax which is modelled in detail
2 marks: Wax rods (runners/vents) are attached; the whole is covered with layers of fine clay to form the mould
2 marks: The mould is heated: wax melts and runs out leaving a cavity
2 marks: Molten metal is poured in; when cool the mould is broken, the core removed and the work chased and polished
5 marks: Any five (1 each): commemorating past Obas/ancestors; recording historical events (plaques); decorating the palace; altar/religious use; showing power and authority of the Oba; royal regalia; diplomatic gifts
questions.explanation: Benin artists also used ivory, wood and terracotta. Lost wax: wax model over a clay core, clay investment, wax melted out, molten brass poured in, mould broken and finished. Court art commemorated Obas, recorded history and displayed royal power.

questions.stem:
Write on the Nigerian artist Bruce Onobrakpeya under the following headings:
(a) background and training; [5 marks]
(b) media and style; [5 marks]
(c) contributions to the development of art in Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Born 1932 at Agbarha-Otor, Urhobo area of present Delta State
3 marks: Trained at the Nigerian College of Arts, Science and Technology, Zaria (late 1950s); member of the Zaria Art Society; later taught art at St Gregory's College, Lagos
3 marks: Media: printmaking (linocut, etching, plastograph, deep etching), painting, bronze lino relief, sculpture/installation
2 marks: Style: semi-abstract, decorative patterns, drawing on Urhobo folklore, myths and traditional motifs
5 marks: Any contributions (1 each, max 5): developed new printmaking techniques; founded the Harmattan Workshop at Agbarha-Otor (1998); trained and mentored many artists; promoted Nigerian folklore/culture internationally through exhibitions; won national/international awards; donated works and wrote on art
questions.explanation: Onobrakpeya (b. 1932, Agbarha-Otor) trained at Zaria and was a member of the Zaria Art Society. He is a printmaker who developed plastography and deep etching, uses Urhobo myth and motifs, and founded the Harmattan Workshop to train artists.

questions.topic: Modern Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem:
(a) Explain how the Oshogbo art movement began, naming two people associated with its founding. [6 marks]
(b) Name two artists of the Oshogbo school. [2 marks]
(c) State seven characteristics of Oshogbo art. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Began in the early 1960s at Oshogbo through workshops and the Mbari Mbayo club
2 marks: Associated founders: Ulli Beier and Georgina Beier (accept Duro Ladipo for Mbari Mbayo club; Susanne Wenger for the Osun grove sculptures)
2 marks: Participants were mainly untrained young people encouraged to work freely from Yoruba myths and daily life
2 marks: Any two (1 each): Twins Seven-Seven, Jimoh Buraimoh, Muraina Oyelami, Rufus Ogundele, Jacob Afolabi, Nike Davies-Okundaye
7 marks: Any seven (1 each): bright, bold colours; themes from Yoruba mythology and folklore; decorative patterns filling the surface; flat figures without perspective; intuitive/untrained approach; use of beads, metal foil, textiles (adire) and printing; repetition of motifs; strong outlines; mixed media
questions.explanation: The Oshogbo school grew out of 1960s workshops run by Ulli and Georgina Beier with the Mbari Mbayo club. Artists such as Twins Seven-Seven and Jimoh Buraimoh used bright colours, Yoruba myths and dense decorative patterns.

questions.stem:
(a) State three beliefs of the ancient Egyptians that influenced their art. [3 marks]
(b) Describe the conventions (rules) followed by Egyptian artists in representing the human figure in wall painting and relief. [8 marks]
(c) Name two famous works of Egyptian art or architecture. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Any three (1 each): life after death; the ka (spirit) needing a likeness/body; the Pharaoh as divine; worship of many gods; preservation of the body (mummification)
2 marks: Head shown in profile while the eye is drawn as seen from the front
2 marks: Shoulders and chest shown frontally; hips, legs and feet in profile
2 marks: Hierarchical scale: important persons (Pharaoh) drawn larger than others
2 marks: Figures arranged in horizontal registers with hieroglyphs; rigid, formal, flat figures with little expression; men darker-skinned than women
4 marks: Any two (2 each): Pyramids of Giza; Great Sphinx; bust of Nefertiti; Tutankhamun's gold mask; temple at Abu Simbel; Palette of Narmer
questions.explanation: Belief in the afterlife and the ka shaped tomb art. Figures follow a fixed convention: profile head with frontal eye, frontal shoulders, profile legs, hierarchical scale, registers. Examples: Giza pyramids, the Sphinx, Nefertiti bust, Tutankhamun's mask.

questions.stem:
(a) What is meant by the term "Renaissance"? [2 marks]
(b) State five characteristics of High Renaissance painting. [5 marks]
(c) Write short notes on Leonardo da Vinci, mentioning two of his works and his contribution to painting technique. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Renaissance means "rebirth": revival of classical Greek and Roman learning and art in Europe, beginning in Italy, c. 14th-16th centuries
5 marks: Any five (1 each): linear perspective; realism/naturalism; anatomically correct figures; chiaroscuro/modelling with light and shade; balanced, pyramidal compositions; humanism; classical and religious themes; oil paint
2 marks: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519): Italian painter, scientist, inventor, the "universal man"
4 marks: Two works (2 each): Mona Lisa; The Last Supper; Virgin of the Rocks; Lady with an Ermine
2 marks: Contribution: sfumato, study of anatomy and nature, atmospheric perspective, pyramidal composition
questions.explanation: The Renaissance was the rebirth of classical ideals from Italy. High Renaissance painting shows perspective, anatomical accuracy, chiaroscuro and balanced compositions. Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper and developed sfumato.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain how Impressionism got its name. [3 marks]
(b) State six characteristics of Impressionist painting. [6 marks]
(c) Name three Impressionist painters and one work by any one of them. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: From Claude Monet's painting "Impression, Sunrise" exhibited in Paris in 1874; a critic used "Impressionists" mockingly and the name stuck
6 marks: Any six (1 each): painting outdoors (en plein air); capturing light and its changing effects; short, broken brushstrokes; bright, unmixed colours placed side by side; coloured shadows (little use of black); everyday scenes as subjects; visible brushwork; open compositions
3 marks: Any three painters (1 each): Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Camille Pissarro, Edgar Degas, Alfred Sisley, Berthe Morisot (accept Manet as associated)
3 marks: One correctly matched work, e.g. Monet: Water Lilies / Impression, Sunrise; Renoir: Luncheon of the Boating Party
questions.explanation: The name came from Monet's "Impression, Sunrise". Impressionists painted outdoors with broken strokes of pure colour to capture fleeting light. Painters: Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Degas.
